speaker: Patrick Hsu
title: Arc Institute's Patrick Hsu on Building an App Store for Biology with AI
question: In drug discovery, why do compounds that succeed in cells and animals still regularly fail when tested in humans?
guest: These are imperfect models. We set up this set of filters in the drug discovery process where first you show it works in cell lines, then you show it works in primary cells or an organoid, then you show it works in a mouse, then you show it works in a monkey, then you test it in people. By the time you've gotten there, five years and $100 million has gone by. That's very challenging, and that's where predictive models will really help. The reason why we do all of these steps in linear series is because we don't have predictive power, so we have to do things in the arena in real life. Growing cells and growing animals takes months to years to actually do those experiments. So the promise of having predictive models isn't just predictive power—it's that you could actually simulate things in a multi-parallelized fashion.

points.core: Preclinical model systems remain fundamentally imperfect proxies for living human biology.
points.note: Accept: cell lines, organoids, mice, and primates fail to fully recapitulate human physiology or disease biology. Do not credit: generic claims that humans are complex without referencing preclinical models as imperfect proxies.

points.core: Lacking predictive power forces teams to run experimental validation steps in linear series.
points.note: Accept: sequential gating/filtering (cell lines -> primary cells/organoids -> mice -> monkeys -> humans) is forced by inability to predict human outcomes upfront. Do not credit: listing preclinical stages without connecting serial testing to lack of predictive power.

points.core: Running sequential biological experiments in living systems takes years before reaching human trials.
points.note: Accept: growing cells and animals takes months to years, consuming roughly 5 years and tens to hundreds of millions of dollars before human testing. Do not credit: vague statements that R&D is slow without tying delay to physical growth/testing cycles of living models.

points.core: Predictive models unlock speed by shifting serial real-world testing into parallelized simulation.
points.note: Accept: trusted predictive models/oracles allow massive parallel in-silico simulation rather than slow serial physical experiments. Do not credit: generic claims that AI speeds up discovery without highlighting parallelized simulation replacing serial testing.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Roughly 90% of drug candidates entering clinical trials fail, mainly because preclinical models are imperfect stand-ins for human disease. The largest share of failures, about half, comes from lack of efficacy: the drug hits its target, but the target turns out not to drive the disease in people. Cell lines and animal models capture only a slice of human biology. A mouse with an engineered tumour or induced Alzheimer's-like pathology does not reproduce the genetic diversity, chronic course, comorbidities, and complexity of the real human condition.

The second major cause, around 30% of failures, is unexpected toxicity. Species differ in metabolism, immune function, and off-target protein interactions, so harm can appear in humans that animals never showed, or the tolerable dose proves too low to work.

The remaining failures stem from poor pharmacokinetics (the drug doesn't reach the right tissue at sufficient concentration for long enough), along with commercial and strategic decisions.

Methodological weaknesses compound all of this: preclinical studies are often small, unblinded, and biased toward positive publication, and trials may enrol the wrong patients or measure the wrong endpoints.

points.why: The response explicitly attributes clinical failures to the limited ability of preclinical models to represent human biology and disease.
quotes: preclinical models are imperfect stand-ins for human disease
Cell lines and animal models capture only a slice of human biology.

points.why: The response does not connect limited predictive power to the need for sequential experimental validation.
The response does not explain how growing and testing living models in sequence adds years before human trials.
The response does not discuss using predictive models to shift serial physical experiments into parallel simulations.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Compounds that succeed in preclinical testing fail in roughly 90% of human clinical trials because cell cultures and laboratory animals imperfectly replicate human biology and disease. Isolated cells lack whole-body context, while animals differ substantially from humans in organ physiology, immune signaling, and metabolic enzymes—such as cytochrome P450s—that govern drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Consequently, a compound with ideal exposure in rodents or primates may fail to reach therapeutic concentrations at its human target or may generate toxic human-specific metabolites.

Moreover, induced animal diseases are usually artificial, acute approximations studied in young, genetically uniform animals under tightly controlled conditions, whereas human illnesses develop over years across genetically diverse patients with comorbidities and concurrent medications. Because of these translational gaps, most clinical candidates ultimately fail from insufficient efficacy, when modulating a target relieves animal symptoms without meaningfully altering human pathology, or from unforeseen safety liabilities and off-target organ toxicities that only emerge in human populations.

points.why: The response directly attributes clinical failures to the limitations of cell cultures and animals as proxies for human biology and disease.
quotes: cell cultures and laboratory animals imperfectly replicate human biology and disease

points.why: The response never connects limited predictive power to the need for sequential experimental validation.
The response gives no account of how growing and testing living models in sequence delays human trials by years.
The response does not discuss using predictive models to replace serial physical experiments with parallel simulations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Roughly 90% of drugs that enter clinical trials never reach approval. Most fail because they don't work well enough in people, which accounts for about 40–50% of failures. Unacceptable toxicity causes about 30%, poor pharmacokinetics around 10–15%, and business decisions make up the rest.

The main cause is that preclinical models are weak stand-ins for human disease. Cell lines are simplified, often heavily mutated systems that lack the tissues, immune system and metabolism of a whole body. Animal "disease" is often created artificially, such as mice engineered to make amyloid for Alzheimer's or given acute injuries to mimic stroke. So a drug can fix the model without touching the real, long-developing human condition. The target itself may also play a smaller role in humans than the models suggested.

Species also differ in drug targets, liver enzymes and immune responses. That can hide toxicity, as when fialuridine (a hepatitis B drug) and TGN1412 (an experimental immune antibody) seriously harmed trial volunteers after animal tests looked safe. It can also mean doses that work in animals don't translate to people.

Lab animals are genetically uniform and housed identically, while patients vary widely in genetics, age, other illnesses and other medications. Finally, many preclinical studies are small, unblinded or hard to reproduce, and positive results get published more often, which makes the early evidence look stronger than it is.

points.why: The candidate explicitly links the limits of preclinical models to the failure of drug effects to carry over to human disease.
quotes: The main cause is that preclinical models are weak stand-ins for human disease.
So a drug can fix the model without touching the real, long-developing human condition.

points.why: The candidate does not explain how limited predictive power forces teams to validate compounds in a fixed sequence.
The candidate does not connect the time required to reach human trials to growing and testing living models in sequence.
The candidate does not discuss using predictive models to replace serial physical experiments with parallel simulations.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Compounds that succeed in cells and animals frequently fail in humans because preclinical models cannot fully capture human biology or real-world disease complexity. Cultured cells lack the intact organs, immune interactions, and blood flow that govern how a drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted in a living body. Animal models are closer, yet species differ significantly in target protein structure, liver enzymes, immune responses, and signaling pathways, meaning a compound can be safe and effective in mice while proving toxic or inactive in people. Moreover, animal studies often rely on genetically uniform, young, healthy subjects with artificially induced conditions that only loosely resemble human diseases, which develop gradually alongside aging, genetic diversity, comorbidities, and other medications. Finally, preclinical experiments frequently suffer from small sample sizes, publication bias, and short observation windows, leaving rare toxicities, off-target effects, and narrow therapeutic windows undetected until larger, longer human trials expose them.

points.why: The response directly attributes clinical failures to the limits of cell and animal models as proxies for human biology.
quotes: preclinical models cannot fully capture human biology or real-world disease complexity

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Cells and animals model only parts of human disease. Cells grown in a dish lack much of the tissue, immune, and hormonal context that shapes a drug’s effects. Animal models capture more of that complexity, but species can differ in how they absorb and metabolize a drug, how its target works, and how the disease develops.

A compound may therefore work in the lab at a concentration that humans can’t safely tolerate, or it may never reach enough of the affected tissue. Even when it reaches and acts on its target, that target may play a smaller role in human disease than the model suggested. Patients also vary in genetics, disease stage, and other medications, and an improvement in a lab measure may never translate into a meaningful benefit for them. Human trials test whether the drug delivers enough benefit at a dose people can safely take.

points.why: The response identifies missing physiological context in cell models and species differences in animal models that limit their relevance to humans.
quotes: Cells and animals model only parts of human disease.
Cells grown in a dish lack much of the tissue, immune, and hormonal context that shapes a drug’s effects.
species can differ in how they absorb and metabolize a drug, how its target works, and how the disease develops.

points.why: The response leaves unexplained how limited predictive power forces teams to validate compounds in successive experimental stages.
The response omits the years spent growing and testing living models in sequence before human trials.
The response omits how predictive models could accelerate discovery by shifting serial physical experiments into parallel simulations.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Cells and animals can show that a compound has a biological effect, but clinical success requires that it improve patients’ health at a dose they can tolerate. A compound may work in cultured cells because they’re exposed directly to a concentration that would be unsafe or impossible to reach in the affected human tissue. People may also break the compound down differently from the test species, reducing its activity or producing a toxic byproduct.

Even when the drug reaches its target and acts as intended, the target may play a smaller role in human disease than the animal model suggested. A change in a laboratory marker may therefore fail to translate into symptom relief or longer survival. Human trials also include patients who differ in disease stage, genetics, and other medications. Those differences can reveal limits on benefit or side effects that small, relatively uniform animal studies missed.

points.why: The response identifies concrete ways that cultured cells and animal models can misrepresent human drug exposure and disease biology.

the target may play a smaller role in human disease than the animal model suggested.
